The dot-com boom didn't start in 1995. It started in 1968.

→ 1980-86: Computer II separates the network from the services running on top of it
→ 1984: AT&T finally broken up into 7 Baby Bells
→ 1986: Computer III forces open architecture

7 transactions per second across the entire global network. Confirmation times measured in tens of minutes when the chain is congested. Fees that spike to $20+ during periods of high activity.

These aren't theoretical use cases. They're waiting for a chain that can actually handle them.

The bull case is: Bitcoin can't do its own job. $KAS can.

Twenty-eight years of infrastructure → four years of mania.

The 28-year groundwork phase compressed into roughly 10 years. The 4-year mania phase compresses into roughly 2 to 3.

Where are we right now? The most defensible answer is somewhere between 1995 and 1998. Definitely not 1992. Probably not 2000 yet. The Netscape moment was ChatGPT. The infrastructure overbuild is happening in the data center cycle. The mania is getting paid for in equity right now.

The Kaspa angle. This matters for $KAS because the runway for accumulating PoW exposure at fair-launch prices is shorter than the four-year cycle crowd assumes.

The Clarity Act stable-coin compromise just landed.

Yield is allowed, but only on accounts with 'material activity' (a payment, a trade). No idle yield. No automatic compounding on parked stables. Both sides left unhappy.

Here's what this means for how you actually deploy capital, and why $KAS becomes the cleaner play once the idle-yield path is gated.

The compromise. The bank lobby pushed for no rewards on idle balances. The crypto side pushed for unrestricted yield. The middle landed at: yield is fine, but the account has to show real usage.

On paper, that sounds like a workable compromise. In practice, it kills the cleanest carry-trade setup we had: park stables on a regulated exchange, earn 4-5% on the float, withdraw when you want to deploy.

That trade required idle yield. Activity-gated yield doesn't replicate it. You'd have to manufacture trades to keep the account 'material', and the cost of those trades will eat the yield in most cases.

Three implications.

First, the compounding-stables crowd has to find a new home. Some of that capital goes to higher-yield DeFi (which carries protocol risk most of those holders won't tolerate). Some goes back into BTC and ETH spot for the optionality. Some goes into PoW alts for the asymmetry.

Second, the idle-yield expectation gets repriced across crypto. If yield on stables requires activity, then 'productive' suddenly looks more attractive on assets that don't pretend to pay yield in the first place. The framing of $KAS as a non-yielding productive asset (deflationary supply curve, hard-capped emission, security budget paid by the protocol itself) becomes the cleaner thesis once the alternative needs a usage gate.

Third, the bear case for the compromise is that it keeps idle stables from becoming a true substitute for treasuries in retail wallets. Which means the capital that would have parked in stables for yield instead has to choose between cash, treasuries, BTC, or PoW alts. None of those are bad outcomes for the asset class.

The Kaspa angle. $KAS doesn't compete with stable yield because it never claimed to. It competes with the asset thesis: capped supply, fair-launch, PoW security, hard-fork milestone in the schedule.

posts.source_transcript: video-creation/longform-edited/media/carry-trade/renders/carry-trade-FINAL.mp4
posts.body:
Japan spent thirty years handing the world free money. That era is ending, and almost nobody is pricing in what happens next.

Here is the part most people miss.

For decades Japan kept interest rates at basically zero. So two very different kinds of money left the country chasing a better return somewhere else. Real money: Japan's own pension funds, life insurers and banks bought foreign bonds and foreign stocks because home paid nothing. Borrowed money: speculators borrowed yen at near zero, converted it, and levered into risk assets, stocks and crypto included.

Both only work while two things stay true. Japan keeps paying nothing, and the yen stays weak. Neither is true anymore.

Japanese bond yields just hit their highest levels since the 1990s. Holding a Japanese bond pays a real return again, and the math that justified sending trillions abroad starts to break. The money is already responding: March 2026 saw the largest monthly inflow ever into Japanese government bond funds, and Japan, the single largest foreign holder of US debt at over a trillion dollars, has started selling.

That drains liquidity out of US markets and crypto at the same time.

Here is the twist for crypto. Japanese pension funds do not hold Bitcoin; their exposure is bonds and stocks. So crypto's risk is indirect through the slow liquidity drain, plus a direct hit if the leveraged side ever squeezes the way it did in August 2024, when $BTC fell from 64K to under 50K in about 48 hours.

If that combination lands while crypto is already soft, it does not start a new crash. It extends the one already underway.

posts.topic: The October bottom is a Mandela effect
posts.source_transcript: transcripts/october-bottom LOW BPS VERTICAL_plain.txt
posts.body:
Everybody remembers 1929 and 1987. Almost nobody remembers the other 97 years.

That one asymmetry created the most feared month in markets, and right now it is quietly setting up the biggest head-fake in crypto.

Here is what October actually looks like in the data since 1927:

- Median return: +1.3%
- 62% of Octobers closed GREEN
- Ranked 6th worst of 12 months, dead middle of the pack
- Volatility: about 36% above the monthly average

So October is not a crash month. It is a volatile month that usually closes positive. Two events spread across 90 years is not a pattern, it is an outlier. September actually carries the weakest record on the calendar, and November and December are among the strongest.

Now map that onto crypto. This cycle is the FIRST time the crypto market has ever carried a mainstream prediction of an October bottom. We have literally never had one before. And the moment 90% of the market believes the bottom lands in October, the trade breaks itself: everybody and their grandma plans to buy back in October, the people who know that plan to buy in September, and the people who know THAT are buying now.

A bottom is the point of maximum fear and minimum demand. You cannot pre-schedule maximum fear for a month when everyone has cash ready and a buy order planned. Their own demand is the reason the real low prints early.

My honest odds: 50% the bottom is already behind us. 40% it prints in the next 30 days, way before October. 10% everything else.

The four-year cycle zombies are running the same playbook one more time. The market has a habit of punishing whatever 90% of participants agree on.
